about: The Country and the city's loop (Docs/Design/68-the-country-and-the-city-loop.md). The Country stands for the farms, mines, woods and villages beyond the walls until they are built: what a keeper draws from the store room is bought from it (its purse is the account outside:<market id>), and every day it spends what it took in on the city's goods, keeping a reserve. `markets` is a list so that the smaller towns can each become a market with its own purse and basket later; there is one for now. A market's `basket` is what its people buy in the city, as shares of its day's spending (any whole numbers; they are scaled to the money it has), weighted toward the trades with time to spare (tools/city_loop.py checks it against the city's makers). `wages` says who pays a post that is neither a shop's keeper nor its hand (those are paid by their shop's till) nor the watch (the treasury): the first rule with a word in the post's title, in lower case. `food` and `comforts` are the residents' buying. The numbers are placeholders; the per-world settings (on and off, the reserve, the toll, the wages, carriage, goods the Country no longer supplies) are the world's own, in live.economy and Atlas's Economy page.

markets.name: the Wharf
markets.people: the country folk not yet placed (Docs/Design/66-worlds-atlas-and-dm.md, 2): when they are given farms, their farms take over the goods they grow

rules.name: the Crown's and the offices' heads
rules.about: The heads of the Crown's household and of the city's offices (doc 68, Progress, "First fixes"): the Queen, the King's daughter, the City Office's head; and ("Trades": the user, 2026-10-31, office heads get a head's pay) the King, the two chancellors, the royal secretary, the Crown's treasurer, the magistrate, the keeper of the rolls (the Records Office), the collector of customs, the warden of the Market Hall, the abbot, the keepers of the Washhouse and the Bathhouse, and the Watch's commander (a guard: the watch's post, at this wage). Paid by the treasury at a keeper's wage (a head's), not a clerk's.

rules.name: the Houses' heads
rules.about: The Minor Houses' family members who run a House's own affairs (doc 68, Progress, "First fixes"): a House's lending, the Grayrock wharf; and the heads of the Houses' offices ("Trades"): the harbourmaster of the Wharf Office, the Counting House's overseer. Kept by their House's estates in the Country (as the Houses' other people), at a keeper's wage.

rules.name: the sea trade
rules.about: Carriage by sea and the Wharf's warehouses: the ships' unloading, the cranes, the carrying up from the wharf, the stores' tallies.

rules.name: the Houses' people
rules.about: The Great and Minor Houses' people, kept by their estates in the Country: heads, stewards, servants, the Houses' own trades.

rules.name: public posts
rules.about: Public posts: the Crown and the Council, the courts, the offices, the Records Office, the customs, the lamps, the markets' hands, the washhouse and baths, the teachers, the abbey, the cathedral and the chapels.

estates.about: The Houses' estates (Docs/Design/72-pulling-the-country-into-the-world.md, Phase 6; the rule `estates`, 1, on): each House's own purse, which collects its lands' rents (the works' surplus and the food farms' land rents, by their `house`; the country workshops' share, by theirs) and pays its own people first, keeping estatePostsDays nights of their wages and its share of the Country's reserve (by its posts' wages) before it buys the Country's basket (the realm's trade beyond it, through the wharf), its House's tables' luxuries and its patrons' work. An estates' post (a `wages` rule with payer `estates`) is the first estate's whose `words` are in its label, in lower case, else the first whose words are in its workplace's cell id, else the one that `grants`. `fund` `wharf`: the estate is the Wharf's purse (outside:wharf; doc 73: the Country's, renamed): Grayrock runs the wharf (doc 67, R28), so the sea trade's takings (the ships' goods, the iron and the lime sold through the store room), the basket and the arrivals stay in it; the others are estate:<id>. The estate that `grants` (the Crown's: its land rents are the realm's grain, herds and salt) keeps the posts no other estate's words match (the Minor Houses, who hold no land in the realm, and the Harrowgates of the King's household) and, each night before the wages, gives any estate short of tonight's posts what it lacks, from what it holds over its own (a grant, the Crown's levy on the realm's land; recorded, never the treasury's). Before its grants it levies the other estates (after estates6, whose Crown granted only yesterday's land rents while the wharf held two nights of its posts and more): what they hold over their own keep, up to what it lacks of its own (its posts' nights and the others' lacks), then, still short of tonight's posts and grants, what they hold over tonight's posts; so every post is paid whenever the estates together hold tonight's. An estate buys only with what it holds over its keep and never more than the estates together hold over the one purse's keep (the reserve and estatePostsDays nights of all their posts), and the Houses' tables together take at most rules.luxuryHousesMost pieces a day. With the rule off every House's money and post is the Country's one purse again, as before Phase 6 (an estate's purse is emptied into it that night); switched on, the Country's money is shared between the estates by their posts' wages.

list.name: House Grayrock's estate (the wharf and the sea trade)

wharf.about: The Wharf (Docs/Design/73-the-wharf.md, 4.2; the user, 2026-11-04: "The wharf 'sells' and 'buys' items from NPC's at whatever is the local, stable price"): the realm's valve to the world beyond it, at the Grayrock Wharf Office on the Wharf Road (its warehouse the Grayrock New Store, the Crown's customs at the Customs House). `imports`: goods of an area the farms grow (or should) that the Wharf lands when the farms can't fill a store draw, the draw's last lot, at most `most` pieces a day realm-wide (times the rule wharfImportScale); every good no area names is the Wharf's anyway, as it was the Country's (the season caps, the world's wharfOff). `takes`: goods the Wharf buys for beyond the realm from the farms and works holding more than wharfKeepDays of their yield (wharfKeepLeast at least), at 16:00, at most `most` a day (times wharfTakeScale), within the beyond's credit. `on` false: listed but off (the new producers' goods, so their own balance shows first; the piles the yields' patch trims). Both at the stable price (the store room's at markup 100, the season's or the area's year factor). A good on both lists, or on `never`, is dropped from both at load. After wharf7b (doc 73, Progress, "Round 1 of stabilizing"): the takes run in this list's order (the foundry's bells first, for its posts' wages; then the farms' piles; then the butchers') and a good the beyond's room can't fit is left for the next, not the end of the run; a take's `shops` (businesses.json ids) are the city's trades it is taken from too, at the stable price and inside the walls (no toll), each shop keeping `keep` pieces (none given: wharfKeepLeast, wharfKeepDays of its sales a day, or its shelf, the most): the butchers' hides and bones, the byproduct of their carcasses that no draw took (~24 of each a day piling, ~5,000 at each of the big butchers by year 3), and the foundry's handbells, its own goods, which no city trade buys (its iron bars the ironworks' since the iron area went on: the foundry idle from year 2); eggs and cider imported when the farms can't fill a draw (supply-bound every season, ~98 and ~18 a day short in wharf7b's year 3), and copper and tin ore, the foundry's bells' metal, which the Frosthollow mine digs at 0.8 and 0.4 a day. Round 2 (doc 73, Progress): cider's most 40 a day (20: the distillery and Marshholm's still, which run it into apple brandy, short ~12 and ~11 a day in stable8's year 1, the realm's two top shortages; the orchards' cider raised by the patch too). `never`: refused whatever a list or a world says (cheese: the user, "Leave cheese as it is").

food.about: Each household goes to market once a day at its own hour, and tops every member up to `days` days of food; one still short of `shortDays` tries again each hour until the shops shut. Food is picked among what the open shops have, the better the nourishment for the price the likelier. Whoever in the household has the money pays.

comforts.about: A household holding more than `above` pennies a head spends `share` of what is over it a day on comforts from the city's shops, used up at once: the better-off buy drink, candles, cloth and treats, so that savings come back to the shops. (Doc 68, Progress, "First fixes": 40p and a fifth, as set 2 measured; at most `rules.comfortsMost` purchases a day.) The day's budget pays for the city's services first (`services`), then comforts. Apple brandy and brandy among them since the still house (doc 72, Progress, "The producers and the fixes"): no household bought either as food (2 nourishment a bottle at 14p and 45p), so the distillery's stood unsold; a comfort is picked only from what an open shop holds, so they take a share of the comforts no bigger than the stills make.

luxuries.about: The luxuries (Docs/Design/72-pulling-the-country-into-the-world.md, Phase 5; the user's decision, 2026-11-03: cheese becomes a comic luxury for wolves, highly desired by all, its price allowed to climb to meet demand so that mostly the rich and noble afford it, but no wolf breaks the bank for it). A luxury is never bought as food. Each household, at its market hour after its food and its needs (the fuel among them; the city's households pay no rent), wants one a head (rules.luxuryMost), bought only from what it holds over its keep, at most rules.luxuryShare percent of that a day: a household of the Houses (by its class) keeps `comforts.above` pennies a head, any other rules.luxuryAbove (after country5, doc 72: the middle class bought nearly all of it, the Houses' wolves holding no more a head than they). The Houses' own tables: once a day the Country's purse (the Houses' estates) buys luxuries with rules.luxuryHouses percent of what it holds over its reserve and its posts' nights, at most rules.luxuryHousesMost pieces, at the shops' own price, before its basket. So the rich and the noble are its buyers; each piece at its shop's own price: a shop's price for a luxury follows its stock as every ware's does (rules.stockPrices) but in its own band, up to rules.luxuryPriceBand percent over the season's price, by rules.luxuryPriceStep thousandths a day, and outside the city's price level (its climb never cheapens the rest). The luxuries' budget comes before the comforts' (out of the same money).

rules.about: The loop's rules the DM can tune (Docs/Design/68-the-country-and-the-city-loop.md, Progress, "First fixes"; each world's own in live.economy.rules, migration 0058, the DM's Economy tab and Atlas's Economy page). comfortsMost: the most comforts a household buys a day (it was 20, which kept the rich from spending their savings). almsADay: pennies a head the city's alms make a household up to after the day's wages (was 7: a day's food with nothing over for a Restday). almsNoEarner (doc 73, Progress, "Round 4 of stabilizing"): a household with no earner (no member holding a paid post: the old, orphans, the out of work, most of them living alone) is made up to this percent of the alms a head, the part over the day's paid only of what the treasury holds over treasuryCap after the short tills' wages (150: half a day's food money over the day's; stable8c's short households held a day's 10p a head and nothing over, a first try at two days' alms, 200, cost ~86p a day more of the alms in the first spring, and one at 150 from the treasury's float as the day's alms ~64p a day in the year's second half, the treasury under its cap and the wage support paid that much less); since round 6 a household whose earners' wages together are under the day's alms a head (a lone hand on a floor wage, a family of four on two hands' wages: most of stable9b's households short in year 3) is made up the same way, after the no-earner's and of what the treasury holds over its cap and tonight's wage support wanted (booked apart, alms_low_wage); 100: as any household. treasuryCap: pennies the treasury keeps; what it holds over this at 18:00, after its own posts, pays what the shops' tills could not pay their posts (wageSupport percent of each till's shortfall; each post the same share of its wage). workBankHours: the crew's hours a shop may bank for a long craft, in hours of the whole crew's work; 0 (the default): as long as the business's longest craft and an hour more (at least two), so a lone cartographer can make a map over two days (was 2, which no 13.9-hour map could fit). fairFood: 1 = at market the members with least food buy first, everyone to `food.shortDays` before anyone to `food.days`, and only foods some member can pay for are picked; 0 = the old order. services: 1 = households buy the city's services (`services`) from their comforts budget; 0 = none. servicesCityShare: the percent of each service's price that goes to the treasury (the city); the rest stays in the shop's till. Trades and the follow-ups (doc 68, Progress, "Trades"): suppliers: 1 = a keeper buys its craft inputs from the city's makers first (`suppliers`: the cooper's casks for the wine makers), at their price, till to till; 0 = all from the store room. patrons: 1 = the trades' patrons (`patrons`: the treasury, the Houses' estates, the wharf) pay for their units' work (the services `for: patrons`) and the armoury's new kit; 0 = none. armourEvery: days between new pieces of kit for each armed wolf. buyAheadDays: days of food more a household buys the day before a Restday or festival (0: none). floatDrawDays: a till's working float, kept back before its wages and its keeper's profit, is its mean draws a day over this many days (1: yesterday's, as it was). floatWagesDays: days of its posts' wages a till keeps over its float before profit (7, a week, as it was). workshopWagesDays (Docs/Design/72-pulling-the-country-into-the-world.md, after country5): a country workshop's, before what is over goes to its House's estate (4 since country6a: Larkfield's smithy, whose float is a day's iron bars, was still short on some Restdays, 98.0% paid; 3 since country5b's carry-overs, with 2 it was short on most; 2 as the works keep floatDays, and the week of floatWagesDays before that). workshopWageMost (doc 72, after country6a): the most pennies a country workshop's wages drift over the world's (its House takes the profit, but the drift, judged on that share, had raised its crews' wages ~130p a day over their base and left the House, the Country's purse, little): 2, a keeper 16p and a hand 10p at most, the works' and the farms' fixed wages; down as any till's. subsidyToNeed: 1 = the carriage subsidy gives the carters only what their till lacks of tonight's wages and its float (nothing to their keeper's profit); 0 = a quarter of all carriage, as it was. estatePostsDays (Docs/Design/72-pulling-the-country-into-the-world.md, Phase 3): the nights of its posts' wages the Country keeps in its purse, over its reserve, before its basket and its patrons buy (2: tonight's and the next's, so a run of lean days never leaves its posts unpaid; it was 1). estates (doc 72, Phase 6): 1 = each House its own estate purse (`estates`): its lands' rents in, its people's wages out, the Crown's grants to an estate short of its posts; 0 = the Country's one purse for them all, as before. landRent (doc 72, open question 2, after country3 showed the Country's intake under its posts): the percent of a food farm's takings it pays each night to the House whose land it is on (into the Country's purse, "the Houses' estates and the sea trade", booked by House: Fell the orchards, vines and hives, Grayrock the fishing, the Crown the grain, herds and salt), after its crew's wages and out of what is over its float, the share its basket would have spent (a farm short of its wages pays none); 16 for every food area without its own: landRentFish 9, landRentFruit 4, landRentGrain 28, landRentSalt 8 (each about half its thinnest farm's margin over its wages in its leanest season of country3's year 3; 0: none); a farm with its own `landRent` in country_farms.json pays that rule instead: landRentDairy 32, the three cattle and dairy farms (doc 72, Phase 4: their margin 67-70% of their takings in country3c's year 3, the pig farms' 41% beside them in the meat area; 24 kept the Country 10% over its posts in its leanest season even if Phase 4 took the 187p a day the doc first put on it; 32 after country5, their margin 68-72% after wages and the Country's summer 8.4% over its posts once the workshops took its sales). The treasury's surplus (doc 68, Progress, "The treasury's surplus: works and alms"): surplus: 1 = at 18:00, last (after the treasury's posts, the short tills' wages and the alms), what the treasury holds over treasuryCap and surplusKeep goes back out; 0 = it stays. surplusKeep: pennies over the cap the treasury keeps for the lean seasons (the toll falls in summer and autumn, below its posts and alms). surplusWorks: percent of the surplus to public works orders from the city's trades (`works`), till to till at the catalogue's price. surplusAlms: percent of it to the poorest households, per head, poorest first, up to surplusAlmsTo pennies a head; what one can't place goes to the other, and what neither places stays. The self-correcting rules (doc 68, Progress, "Self-correcting rules"; each gentle, each its switch; what each has drifted to is saved with the society and shown, read only, beside the rules): stockPrices: 1 = a shop's price for a ware follows its stock, up stockPriceStep thousandths a day when it sells out, down as much when more than three days of the day's sales are left over its starting stock (the season's stock-up allowed for), else a quarter step back toward the catalogue's; then the day's factors are scaled so their mean, weighted by sales, is 1 (what is scarce dearer against what is plentiful, the city's prices as a whole the catalogue's); within stockPriceBand percent of the catalogue's (the season's) price, and never under what the store room charges the shop for the ware and a twentieth; on top of the season's price, paid as it is; players pay it too (and a shop offers them SellBackShare of it), the Country's purchases stay at the catalogue's. shelfFollow: 1 = a ware's shelf is shelfCover percent of its sales a day smoothed over about shelfDays days, never under its starting stock; a day it sells out having sold at least its shelf counts as shelfGrow percent more than its shelf (at most 1,000), so a shelf too small to show its demand grows; a Restday's or festival's few sales never lower it; 0 = a quarter more than yesterday's sales, as it was. wageDrift: 1 = every wageDriftDays days a till that paid all its posts every day, its keeper's profit at least wageDriftSpare percent of their wages, raises each post's wage a penny, and one short on more than half of them lowers it a penny, never under wageDriftFloor pennies (a day's food) and at most wageDriftMost either way on a keeper's wage, wageDriftHandMost on a hand's (12 each, from 6: doc 68, Progress, "Players in the shifting market; wider wages; the long runs"); the treasury's and the Country's posts keep their wages. treasuryDrift: 1 = the treasury's level, a slow mean of it at 18:00 over about treasuryDays days, is judged every treasuryJudgeDays days (28; it was a fortnight) against treasuryTarget (5,500p, about where it settles; it was 5,000p: doc 68, Progress, "Births follow deaths; arrivals from the Country; the treasury's target"): over it and treasuryBand percent and not falling, the gate toll eases tollStep tenths of a point and the alms rise a penny a head; under it and not rising, the toll firms and the alms tighten; first judged once the level has had treasuryDays to settle; the toll at most tollDriftMost points from the world's (1 since doc 73's round 10, the user asking again on 2026-11-06 to soften it; 2 since doc 73's round 9, the user's decision of 2026-11-05 to soften the drift: at 5 the toll firmed every season to 35, as the treasury never nears its target, and moved the estates' land and works rents to the treasury year on year; at 2 it stops at 32 in year 2 and the Crown's margin over its keep is level in year 3; round 10 measured 0, 1 and a slower step, 0.2, beside 2 on three years: at 1 the toll stops at 31 on day 238 and the Crown's and Timberland's margins are level in year 3, where at 2 they eased 2% and 6%, for some 20p a day less of the wage support paid and fewer of the no-earner's and low wage's alms; at 0 a third of the support goes unpaid; at 0.2 the toll still firms in year 3), the alms up to almsDriftMost pennies over almsADay and never under it (the line under hunger). The surplus stays the nightly ceiling; this is the slow trim under it. farmSurplus (Docs/Design/73-the-wharf.md, Progress, "Round 1 of stabilizing"): 1 = a food farm's basket spends at most its design's a day (country_farms.json `basketADay`), and once it has paid its crew what its till holds each night over its float and that is its House's, as a works' surplus is (wharf7b: the dairies', the grain farms' and two orchards' baskets ~237p a day over their design while the estates' posts went short on 107 nights); 0 = its basket spends all it holds over its float and tonight's wages and rent. shopRot (doc 73, Progress, "Round 2 of stabilizing"): 1 = a maker's perishable by-product (a good its crafts make and none of them uses, not food, that keeps only so many days: items.json `keeps`, the butchers' hides) held over its keep (the Wharf's for a shop: wharfKeepLeast, wharfKeepDays of its sales, its shelf) loses a keeps-th of what is over each night, as hides rot untanned (stable8: ~19 a day piling, 18,835 at the butchers by year 3); 0 = it keeps. landRentThin (doc 72, Phase 5, country4's carry-over): the land rent of the thinnest farms (country_farms.json `landRent` "thin": the two lake boats, the two salt works, orchards 2, 4 and 5, 5-8p a day over their wages and rent in country4's year 3, orchard_5 short two nights), 0: none. The luxuries (doc 72, Phase 5, the user's decision; `luxuries`): luxuryShare, the most percent of what a household holds over its keep a head that it spends on luxuries a day, after its food and needs; luxuryMost, the most pieces a head a day; luxuryAbove (after country5: the middle class bought 11.5 a day, the Houses' wolves 0.1, both holding ~50p a head), the keep a head of a household not of the Houses, by its class (the Houses' households keep comforts.above); luxuryHouses, the percent of what the Country's purse holds over its reserve and its posts' nights that it spends a day on luxuries for the Houses' own tables (its basket's money, before the basket), at the shops' own price, at most luxuryHousesMost pieces a day; luxuryPriceBand, how far over the season's price a shop's price for a luxury may climb, in percent (700: eight times; it was 300); luxuryPriceStep, thousandths a day it climbs when the shop sells out (and falls on a glut, a quarter of it back toward the season's on a quiet day).

steering.about: Steering the economy (Docs/Design/74-steering-the-economy.md; Docs/Design/75-the-economy-controller.md). The rules steer (on/off) and steerLean (the DM's slider, "Where the money rests": 0 shared, 100 today's economy, 200 held by the rich; the tab shows -100 to +100) set where the levers below are read, x from -1 to +1, straight lines between the five marks (-1, -0.5, 0, +0.5, +1). null at the centre or an end is the world's own value of that rule, and at a half mark halfway between its two neighbours, so a measured end blends in with |x| from the world's own at the centre (doc 75, 3.2): at x 0 every lever is the world's own, and the centre is today's economy to the penny. The slider moves the levers the same night; nothing trims them (doc 75 took doc 74's push and its judging, the share-out, the toll lean, the rent scale and the hunger pulls away). The levers: levelling, the Levelling tithe, percent of the way each resident household's cash a head moves to the head-weighted mean each night after the alms (those over it pay, those under it are given, through fund:relief; never a till, farm, estate or the treasury; whole pennies, the remainders the largest first); charters, the Crown's charters, percent of the middle keepers' city tills (a keeper's till that is not a House's, its keeper's household not upper class, by its 28-night mean profit) chartered to the House whose district it is in (else the Crown): the keeper is paid its wage and the profit goes to the House; the till keeps a keeper's till's float, wage days and wage bound; a change in their number is reached in equal nightly steps over chartersRampDays nights (once the keepers' profit has had 28 nights), handed back newest first, and all at once when the steering is turned off; postsShare, percent of a city keeper's nightly profit to the shop's other posts; surplusKeep, treasuryCap and surplusAlmsTo, the treasury's surplus rules; treasuryTarget, the toll drift's target (the world's 5,500p at the centre; at the ends a level the treasury reaches there); groundRent, percent of a city keeper's nightly profit to the Crown's estate (to the treasury instead while the treasury, on its 28-night mean or that night, is under treasuryFloor); dividend, percent of the estates' spare to the upper-class households each night, plus dividendPerCharter points for each point of charters; richAbove, the comforts' keep a head for upper-class households (pennies); spendAbove, the comforts' keep a head for every other household (pennies), so the levelled money comes back to the shops. The end marks of levelling, charters and treasuryTarget are provisional until the calibration (doc 75, 5.2) writes them. The targets (at the slider): gini and giniBand, the earners' Gini; upper and upperBand, the upper share (percent of all the money held by upper-class households, the Houses' estates and the Houses' tills, chartered ones among them); upperMost, top10Most and top10Least, watched only; hungerMost, hungry residents an hour (28-night mean), and shortMost, households short a day. neverHungry and neverBroke, the two floors, work whatever the steering does: a wolf under a day's food at 17:00 (a farm's crew among them) is given food up to it at the stable price from a shop's stock (else the Wharf's), and a household under its next day's necessities at 18:00, after the alms, is given just enough; both paid by the skim, never minted. The skim (doc 74, 6, "The skim reworked") takes idle money first, in a set order of payers (skimOrder, by name: estates, the estates' spare over their keep for their posts; treasury, over its cap and tonight's wage support, never at 17:00; upper, upper-class households; keepers, the keepers' households, not upper or lower class and not a chartered shop's; middle, other middle-class households); lower-class households never pay, and a household pays only on what it holds over comfortable times its necessities a head (and never under the comforts' keep). Within each step the richest first, judged afresh, weighted by how long the money has sat: each holder's idle spare rises toward its spare by 1/idleDays of the gap a night and falls at once; the first pass takes at most skimMost percent of each holder's idle spare, step by step; the second, short of it, up to the whole of each spare, step by step again. Never Broke's top-up is credit toward necessities (the household's food and needs at the shop, drawn from fund:relief as it buys), not cash; credit unused by the next night is not drawn again. With Never Broke on, while the tills short's 28-night mean is over tillsShortNormal (the centre's level) by more than tillsShortOver percent, the first pass takes the estates' and the treasury's whole spare before any household's. Doc 75, D1 (Batch 0, 2026-11-06): skimOrder the treasury, upper, keepers, middle and the estates last; comfortable 2 (was 4); the guard off (tillsShortOver 1000). Doc 75, Phase 3's calibration and Phase 4: levelling 50 at -1 (L50) and 13.7 at -0.5 (the measured curve); charters 33 at +1 (R33, the coordinator's call); treasuryTarget 1,400p at -0.5 (a level the treasury reaches there; the blend's 3,500p pinned the toll up), and the world's own (5,500p) right of the centre, so the toll holds its point there as at the centre (Phase 4's smoke S2: float days 12 to 2); treasuryCap 980p at +1 (the plan's target x 1.15; smoke S3: the wage support unpaid 275p to 140p a day). The safety supervisor (doc 75, 3.6), nightly after the steering's measures, on 7-night means once they have had 7 nights: 1 the treasury under its floor (treasuryFloors: each mark's 13 months of 28 days, its calibration run's seasonal profile less 2 sigma, sigma at least stable10b's 191p, never under supervisor.floorLeast; a null half mark halfway between its neighbours): the ground rent to the treasury in proportion to the gap (all of it at routeAt of the floor under it; beside treasuryFloor's own route), the skim leaves the treasury be, the rich hold eases; 2 the tills short over tillsOver x the mark's tillsShort, or the wage support unpaid over unpaidMost: the tithe eases titheShopsWeek points a week (left), the rich hold richShopsWeek pennies (right); 3 hungry residents over hungerMost or households short over shortMost (each with its floor off): the tithe eases titheHungerWeek (left), chartersHungerWeek charters a week handed back, newest first (right); 4 a lever backed off edgeNights nights running: at the envelope's edge, logged only. A rule fires only where it has a lever to move and clears under clearShare of its trigger for clearNights nights running; each lever moves once a night at the fastest rule's rate and returns at returnShare of the rate it left, never past the world's own value. Doc 75, Phase 5's first fix round (after acceptance A1-A9): treasuryCap 1,300p at +1 tried (980p held the treasury at its 600p floor, so rule 1 never cleared: on 178 nights running in A5; at 1,300p the treasury rose only 70p and the wage support unpaid 152p to 282p, float days 6 to 20) and back to 980p, and 1,490p at +0.5 (as it was, by the blend); unpaidMost 426p, 1.3 x T6's 328p, as the tills short's 1.3 (at 328p a 7-night mean of a seasonal measure fired on an annual bar); returnShare 1 (a lever back at the rate it left: at half, one month's back-off is three at a back-off); the +0.5 floor from A4, its own mark's profile under this table (halfway between the centre's and +1's put the centre's winter floor, about 1,000p, under a treasury that holds about 1,000p there). D3 (doc 75, 7): the right end fails acceptance with the charters (R33: T3, T5, T8 after the fix round; the supervisor on 52-66% of nights, the treasury at its floor), so it ships F1, the right without charters: charters 0 at +1 (built, unused), the dividend 30% at +1 (the ladder's F1), the rest as above. reach: the slider's ends labelled with what they were measured to deliver (doc 75, Phase 6: re-centred on years 2-3 of the 3-year confirmation runs, as 3.5 says: A1 0.061 through the day, the centre 0.344; A5 at F1 22.9%, the centre 12.9%; Phase 5's year 1 was 0.066 and 21.8%).

reach.left: Shared: Gini 0.06 through the day (cash a head over all households; 0.34 at the centre)
reach.right: Held by the rich: about 23% of all money with the upper class and the Houses (13% at the centre)

services.about: The city's services (the user, 2026-10-31: "Make them public services that NPC's have the occasional need to purchase from, but make it items that NPC's buy when they have excess money that isn't needed for other things. The money goes partly to the shop owner and to the city."). Each is a catalogue item (category service, items.json: its name and its price) a business does for a household: bought only from the household's comforts budget (what is over `comforts.above` a head, after food, needs and their reserve), at its market hour, about once every `every` days (a fixed roll of the household and the day: nothing saved), from an open shop of `business` in its community (else anywhere open). Done at once: nothing is kept on a shelf or at home. Of its price `rules.servicesCityShare` percent goes to the treasury, the rest to the shop's till. Each world may turn one off or change its price and frequency (live.economy.services). A service `for: patrons` (doc 68, Progress, "Trades") is never a household's: it is done for each unit of its business's patrons (`patrons`: an armed wolf, a hull, a building) about once every `every` days, paid by the patron, with no city share.

suppliers.about: The city's makers that supply another business's craft inputs first (doc 68, Progress, "Trades"; the rule suppliers): what a `buyer`'s keeper draws for its crafts it buys from a `seller`'s till holding it, at the seller's price (the catalogue's, a dearer season's after), till to till inside the walls (no toll, no carriage), and from the store room only what the city's sellers lack. `goods`: the goods it covers (none: every input the seller sells). A good a shop sells on (doc 72, Phase 5: the resale path) is bought the same way, from the city's makers and the country workshops first, but at the store room's price for it (resaleMarkup of the season's, so the reseller's costs never rise; `price`, a percent of the catalogue's, where a maker would sell under its inputs' cost at that: the smiths' nails and cookpots and the bandages at the catalogue's). The wine makers' casks from the cooper (wine by the cask: crafts.json); and since doc 72's Phase 4 (Docs/Design/72-pulling-the-country-into-the-world.md, 4.5) the craft inputs the Country's store sold the city's makers: linen cloth from the weaver (its flax from the grain farms), iron hoops from the smithies and the cooperage, planks from the Timberland Sawmill, cord from the chandlery (its hemp from the grain farms), paper from the papermill and the scriptorium, leather from the tannery, ink from the scriptorium and the printing house. A maker's own input (the chandlery's cord for its candles) stays the store room's, but for the ropewalk's (after country5b, doc 72: the ropewalk makes cord too, crafts.json, and sells it the chandleries, the soapworks, the general stores, the jeweller, the tinker and the fletcher; the builders' works and the carpenters sell their planks beside the sawmill: the Country still sold ~26 cord and ~2 planks a day while the ropewalk and the builders' works stood idle on the wage support). Phase 5 (doc 72, 4.6, the country workshops, Data/Economy/workshops.json): Coldwater's soap boiler and chandler (fine soap for the general stores, its cord from the chandlery and the ropewalk), its wool weavers (scarves for the rag-and-bone men), Larkfield's linen weavers (linen beside the city's weaver, and for the presses), the presses and paper mills of Larkfield and Oakhaven (pamphlets for the general stores, paper for the printing house and the cartographer, their ink from the scriptorium and the printing house), the potteries of Fenshore and Southmeadow (clay pots), Larkfield's village smithy (hoops beside the smithies and the cooperage; nails and cookpots); and the doc's leftovers from the city's makers: the general store's and the builders' yard's nails, the rag-and-bone man's and the pawnbroker's cookpots, the barber's bandages. The iron (doc 72, Progress, "Iron and lime out of the Country"): every maker of iron goods (the smithies, Larkfield's smithy, the cooperage, the cartwright, the tinker, the builders' works, the armoury, the saddlery, the fletcher) buys its wrought iron from the city's Timberland Ironworks and the foundry, which smelt it of the Frosthollow mine's ore and the Upper hearths' charcoal (the iron area, country_farms.json); while the iron area is on the store room sends none. The producers and the fixes (doc 72, Progress, after iron6): the city's weaver buys its linen for its neckerchiefs from Larkfield's linen weavers too (it drew a trace of the Country's), the jeweller its copper bars from the foundry (of the Frosthollow mine's copper ore; it drew ~0.3 a day of the Country's), and the vintner its brandy and apple brandy from the Coldwater Still House (House Fell's) and the distillery (its aqua vitae too). Round 2 of stabilizing (Docs/Design/73-the-wharf.md, Progress, "Round 2 of stabilizing"): the butchers' by-products to the trades that use them, which drew them from the farms while the butchers' piled (~19 hides and ~23 bones a day by stable8's year 3, their carcasses' cost paid and the by-products never sold): the tannery's hides, the inns' bones for their stew, the general stores', the jeweller's and the tinker's bones for their charms; and the foundry's bronze bars to the smiths and the jeweller and its tin bars to the glassworks (the Wharf landed them). Later chains, such as the mill's flour for the bakers, are a line here. Round 4 of stabilizing (doc 73, Progress, "Round 4 of stabilizing"): the smaller iron trades (the cooperage, the cartwright, the tinker, the builders' works, the armoury, the saddlery and the fletcher, ~4 bars a day in stable8c's year 3) buy their wrought iron of the foundry alone, the smithies and Larkfield's smithy of either: a seller is picked by the stock it holds, so the ironworks' larger shelves took every order and the foundry, House Timberland's too, sold ~0.2 bars a day once the Wharf stopped taking its bars (its takings 92, 26, 15p a day over the three years).

houseBusinesses.about: The Houses' businesses in the city whose profit is their House's, not their keeper's (Docs/Design/72-pulling-the-country-into-the-world.md, Progress, "The producers and the fixes"; the user, 2026-11-04: "sending the ironwork's and foundry profits to their owning estate" rather than a treasury lever): a till whose keeper's post works at one of these buildings (`building`, the map's interior id) is run as a country workshop is (workshops.json): its posts are paid their wages, which drift at most rules.workshopWageMost over the world's; what the till holds each night over its float and rules.workshopWagesDays of its wages goes to `house`'s estate (its House's own purse since Phase 6), booked by House with the works' rents and the workshops' shares. The Timberland Ironworks and the Timberland Foundry (House Timberland's since doc 67's renames; their ids keep doc 61's names), which smelt the Frosthollow mine's ore since the iron left the Country. The other House-owned businesses in the city that could follow (the map's territories; not listed here, so their keepers keep their profit): House Timberland's Anchor Forge and Nailers' Forge (smithies), the Rivet and Rain (the armoury), the Charcoal Store and the Sawmill; House Greatly's Plasterworks, Colour Works, Masons' Yard, Yard and Bank; House Grayrock's ropewalk.

patrons.about: The trades whose customers are the city, the Houses and the wharf rather than households (doc 68, Progress, "Trades"; the user, 2026-10-31, on the armoury: "Armory should have houses and city as customers ... high cost items replaced occasionally, but repaired frequently which should be the main source of their business"; and the follow-ups: the shipwright's hulls for the wharf and sea carriage, the builders' yard's upkeep of the public buildings and the Houses' halls). Each group is a patron with its units: the posts of `roles` (the watch: every guard's post), else `units` (not placed: a number); `payer` the treasury or a market's id (the Houses' estates and the wharf are the Country, as with the Houses' wages). Once a day, at the first hour one of the trade's shops is open, each unit has each of the trade's services `for: patrons` done about once every `every` days (their prices and frequencies: `services`, the DM's), and where the trade has `pieces`, a new piece bought about once every rules.armourEvery days (one of these the shop holds, at the catalogue's price). A payer spends only what it can spare: the treasury over its float and tonight's posts, the Country over its reserve and its posts.

groups.name: the Houses' armed retainers (their estates: none placed yet, a number)
the wharf's and sea carriage's hulls (the Wharf)

works.about: The city's public works (doc 68, Progress, "The treasury's surplus: works and alms"; the user, 2026-10-31): with its surplus (rules.surplus, surplusWorks) the treasury buys upkeep and goods for the public buildings and services from the city's businesses, at their (the catalogue's) price, till to till. Each trade has `weight` shares of the day's orders (of what is left: what one can't place goes on to the next), spread so that the money becomes wages rather than one owner's profit: a trade's tills with most room under their keeper's profit (their float and a week of their posts' wages) first. `goods`: a service (the builders' yard's work on the public buildings) is done at once; a good comes off the shop's shelves (one left for its customers) and is used up in the works, so the shop makes more.

shelves.about: Dear goods a shop keeps fewer of on its shelves than the usual four (doc 68, Progress, "Trades"): theriac, the apothecary's rare cure-all, one at a time.

seasons.about: The seasons in the Country's supply (Docs/Design/68-the-country-and-the-city-loop.md, Progress, "Seasons and the DM's rules"): each group's goods, and for Spring, Summer, Autumn and Winter (the value at each season's middle day; the days between blend in a straight line), in percent of normal: `supply`, how much the Country can send the city a day, of `normal` pieces a day for the whole group (0 pieces: no cap; a supply of 0 sends none); `price`, what the group's goods cost, both the shops' draws from the store room and the shops' prices to residents (the residents weigh nourishment for the price, so they buy what is in season); `shelf`, how full the shops keep their shelves of the group's goods (a maker stocking up ahead of a lean season). Goods made of a group's goods sit in it when their price should follow it (bread with the grain). The numbers are placeholders, each world's to change in the DM (its Economy tab) or Atlas's Economy page; `normal` is about what the city drew a day without a cap (build 48).

groups.name: grain and flour
groups.about: Harvested late summer into autumn: plentiful and cheap then, so more bread; dearer and short in winter and spring until the next harvest.

groups.name: fresh fruit
groups.about: Apples, berries and grapes: plentiful from high summer to the autumn's end, scarce in winter.

groups.name: fresh fish
groups.about: More fresh fish in winter (the user's call, 2026-10-31): the cold months' catch.

groups.name: livestock and meat
groups.about: Kept the year round: no season.

groups.name: milk and dairy
groups.about: The year round, a little less (and dearer) in winter.

groups.name: honey
groups.about: Taken from summer into autumn; scarcer in winter and spring.

groups.name: dried and preserved fruit
groups.about: The preserver's goods keep for months and don't follow the season themselves: their makers stock up in autumn, while fruit is cheap and plentiful (their shelves run to 2.5 times their sales), so there is more of them through the winter, when fresh fruit is scarce (their shelves fall back to normal by spring, so the stock is sold down before more is made). Since doc 68's follow-ups ("winter preserves"): the Country's own stores (`stores`) send them when fresh fruit runs short, a preserver that can't make them for the fruit's cap drawing them itself (at most `normal` pieces a day times `supply`: most in winter, little in summer), and they are a tenth cheaper in winter, so residents eat more of them then, beside the winter's fresh fish.
